advances: An ordinary Lebesgue-volume bound at a specified interior mark. The inverse-energy certificate is dominated by the existing physical retained-mass guarantee; no mixed selection or sum of own-fiber payments follows.

proof:
Translate $y$ to zero. By accepted fact efa4558174ce60cf, the optimal density is the indicator of the convex cap $D=K\cap\{1+u\cdot x\ge0\}$ for a minimizing normalized hinge parameter $u$, and $D$ has volume $T$ and centroid zero. Also $T=V$ exactly at the centroid. The constant energy parameter gives $E\le V$. It is optimal exactly at the centroid, because the energy objective is differentiable and strictly convex on its open convex admissible parameter set, and its gradient at zero is $-(d+1)\int_K x\,dx$. Thus the case $T=V$ is settled. For $d=1$, write $K=[-\ell,r]$; the interval formulas of efa4558174ce60cf, $T=2\min(\ell,r)$ and $E=4\ell r/(\ell+r)$, give $E/V=2\tau-\tau^2$. For the proper retained cap case in $d\ge2$, the cutting plane meets the interior of $K$ and $u\ne0$.

Use the height $t=u\cdot x$. Let $f(t)=\mathcal H^{d-1}(K\cap\{u\cdot x=t\})/|u|$ on the projection interval $[A,B]$, and zero elsewhere. Then $\int f=V$, $A<-1<0<B$, and
$$
\int_{-1}^B f(t)\,dt=T,\qquad \int_{-1}^B t f(t)\,dt=0.
$$
The root $f^{1/(d-1)}$ is concave on $(A,B)$ by Minkowski inclusion of interpolated sections and Brunn–Minkowski. For a highest point in $D$, its homothety of $D$ of ratio $(B-s)/(B+1)$ is contained in the portion of $D$ at height at least $s$, for $-1\le s\le B$. Integrating this lower bound for the height survival function under uniform measure on $D$ gives $1=\mathbb E_D(t+1)\ge (B+1)/(d+1)$, so $B\le d$.

Write $N=d+1$ and $g(t)=(dT/N)((d-t)/N)^{d-1}$ on $t\le d$. On $[-1,d]$ it has mass $T$ and centered moment zero: under its normalized law there, $(d-t)/N$ has density $d s^{d-1}$ on $[0,1]$ and mean $d/N$. The positive set of $f-g$ in $(-1,d)$ is an interval up to endpoints, because $f^{1/(d-1)}-g^{1/(d-1)}$ is concave on $(A,B)$ and $f=0$ beyond $B$. If the two laws differ on a positive-measure set, their matched mass forces a nonempty positive interval $(r_1,r_2)$. Its endpoints satisfy $-1<r_1<r_2<d$: if $r_1=-1$, then $(t-r_2)(f-g)$ is nonpositive and strictly negative on a positive-measure set, contradicting the matched moments. If $r_2=d$, use $(t-r_1)(f-g)$, which is nonnegative and strictly positive on a positive-measure set. For any convex function $w$ finite on $[-1,d]$, subtract its secant at $r_1,r_2$. The affine term integrates to zero against $f-g$, and the remaining product with $f-g$ is nonpositive. Therefore $\int_{-1}^d w f\le\int_{-1}^d w g$, with equality for strictly convex $w$ only if the laws agree almost everywhere. This also holds if the laws already agree.

The same root difference is nonpositive at $-1$ by continuity in the actual interior. Concavity between a point left of $-1$ and a point in $(r_1,r_2)$ implies $f\le g$ to the left of $-1$. In the equal-law case the root difference vanishes at $-1$ and at interior positive-side heights, giving the same conclusion. Outside $[A,B]$ on the left the conclusion follows from $f=0$. Put $\eta=\tau^{1/d}\in(0,1)$ and $a_0=d-N/\eta<-1$. The truncation $\psi=g\mathbf1_{[a_0,d]}$ has total mass $T((d-a_0)/N)^d=V$. Thus on $(-\infty,-1)$ the densities $f$ and $\psi$ have equal mass. The sign of $f-\psi$ is nonnegative below $a_0$ and nonpositive above it in that range. Subtracting the value $w(a_0)$ from any increasing test function yields $\int_{t<-1}w f\le\int_{t<-1}w\psi$, with equality for a strictly increasing test only when the two laws agree there almost everywhere.

Take $c=(\eta-1)/(N-d\eta)<0$ and $w(t)=(1+ct)^{-N}$. Its endpoint denominators at $d$ and $a_0$ are $L_d=1/(N-d\eta)$ and $L_{a_0}=1/\eta$, respectively. Since $B\le d$ and $c<0$, $cu$ is admissible on all of $K$ and $w$ is strictly increasing and strictly convex on the supports. The two comparisons give
$$
E\le\int f w\le\int\psi w
=\frac{V}{L_d L_{a_0}^d}=V(N-d\eta)\eta^d.
$$
The integral follows by setting $s=(d-t)/(d-a_0)$ and differentiating $s^d/[L_d(L_d+(L_{a_0}-L_d)s)^d]$ on $[0,1]$.

Equality forces $f=\psi$ almost everywhere, hence $[A,B]=[a_0,d]$ by positivity of interior sections. The sections at interior heights approach the endpoint sections in Hausdorff distance: compactness gives the upper inclusion in the limit, and interpolating the endpoint section with a fixed interior point gives the lower inclusion. Thus the bottom section has the prescribed positive volume, using volume continuity for compact convex sets. The cone from that bottom section to any highest point is contained in $K$ and its volume equals $V$, by the section profile. Proper containment of full-dimensional compact convex bodies would leave positive volume, so this cone is $K$. The retained subcone cut at $-1$ has centroid zero; hence the mark lies on its axis strictly above the full body's centroid toward the apex.

Conversely in such an axial cone, a proper subcone homothetic to $K$ about the apex has centroid $y$. Its indicator attains $T$, by the pointwise hinge bound for the affine cut normalized to equal one at $y$. In this height chart the section law is $\psi$. For a variable axial coefficient $c'$ the energy integral is $V/[(1+c'd)(1+c'a_0)^d]$ by the same integral. Its derivative vanishes at $c$, since $d/L_d+d a_0/L_{a_0}=0$. The section centroids relative to $y$ are linear in $t$ on the axis, so zero weighted height moment makes the full energy gradient zero, giving the full minimum by convexity. All $\tau\in(0,1)$ are obtained by varying the apex homothety ratio in $(0,1)$.

Differentiation gives $F_d'(\alpha)=((d+1)^{d+1}/d^d)(1-(d+1)\alpha^{1/d}/d)$, so $F_d$ is strictly increasing with $F_d(0)=0$, $F_d(\Gamma_d)=1$. The substitution $F_d(\Gamma_d\tau)=N\tau-d\tau^{1+1/d}$ proves the equivalent certificate inequality. By accepted fact 6769574fc1bd9f8d, the maximizing density puts $y$ in the mass-$T$ metronoid, so a closed containing cap of fraction $\alpha$ has $\alpha\ge\Gamma_d\tau$. For $\alpha\le\Gamma_d$ this proves $E/V\le F_d(\alpha)$.

For the equality direction, let $d\ge2$, $\alpha<\Gamma_d$, and suppose $E/V=F_d(\alpha)$. Both inequalities must be equalities, giving the axial retained cone and $\alpha V=\Gamma_d T$. In the normal of this through-mark halfspace, take the top cap $A'$ of $K$ of volume $T$. The directional bathtub proof of 6769574fc1bd9f8d gives $u'\cdot g_{A'}\ge u'\cdot y$ for the cap normal $u'$. If the inequality were strict, a positive-volume slab in $A'$ between these levels would make the original cap strictly larger than the cap of $A'$ through $g_{A'}$, which has volume at least $\Gamma_d T$ by the same fact with full mass on $A'$. The slab is positive because the centroid level is in the interior of the projection interval of the full-dimensional $A'$. Thus the levels agree and the maximizing density $\mathbf1_D$ of mass $T$ attains the directional bathtub optimum. Equality in its pointwise comparison forces $\mathbf1_D=\mathbf1_{A'}$ almost everywhere, because the height threshold plane is null. Both are full-dimensional compact convex bodies, so $D=A'$. A proper cap's cutting plane and retained side are determined by its interior trace in $K$, so the through-mark cap is toward the apex and parallel to the base. Conversely, for each such axial mark the cap through $y$ toward the apex has volume $\Gamma_d T$ by homothety from the retained cap's base to its centroid level. At the centroid the analogous parallel apex cap captures $\Gamma_d V$. These caps are globally minimal by 6769574fc1bd9f8d, and sharpness follows by varying the axial mark. The equality statement at $\alpha=\Gamma_d$ follows from $E=V$ exactly at the centroid. In $d=1$, the smaller side has fraction $\alpha\le1/2$, and the interval formula gives $E/V=4\alpha(1-\alpha)$.

Tightening a closed containing halfspace to pass through $y$ can only decrease its volume; the minimum over unit normals exists by continuity, since the cutting hyperplanes are null. If this minimum is at most $\Gamma_d$, invert the containing-cap bound; otherwise the inverse is at most $\Gamma_d$ since $E\le V$. On $(0,\Gamma_d]$, $-F_d''(\alpha)\ge((d+1)/d)^{2d+1}$, and $F_d'(\Gamma_d)=0$. Integrating twice gives $F_d(\alpha)\le1-\frac{d+1}{2d}(1-\alpha/\Gamma_d)^2$. Combining with the containing-cap bound when the minimum is at most $\Gamma_d$ proves the square-root estimate; otherwise that estimate holds since its right side is at most $\Gamma_d$. In dimension one the quadratic identity gives exactness.
statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, be a compact full-dimensional convex body, and let $y\in\operatorname{int}K$. Set $V=|K|$, let $E=E_K(y)$ be the minimum of $\int_K[1+a\cdot(x-y)]^{-d-1}\,dx$ over affine denominators positive on $K$, and let $T=T_K(y)$ be the greatest mass of a density in $[0,1]$ on $K$ with centroid $y$. Put $\tau=T/V$. Then
$$
\frac EV\le (d+1)\tau-d\tau^{1+1/d}.
$$
In dimension one there is equality for every interval and interior mark. For $d\ge2$, at $\tau=1$ the mark is the centroid and there is equality. For $\tau<1$, equality holds exactly when $K$ is a cone over a full $(d-1)$-dimensional convex base and $y$ lies on the axis joining the base centroid to the apex, strictly between the body centroid and the apex. Every $\tau\in(0,1]$ occurs at equality.

Put $\Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d$ and $F_d(\alpha)=((d+1)^{d+1}/d^d)\alpha(1-\alpha^{1/d})$ for $0\le\alpha\le\Gamma_d$. This function increases strictly onto $[0,1]$. The energy inequality is equivalent, with the same equality cases, to $V F_d^{-1}(E/V)\le\Gamma_d T$. If a closed halfspace through $y$ captures a fraction $0<\alpha\le\Gamma_d$ of $V$, then $E/V\le F_d(\alpha)$. In dimension one this is equality. For $d\ge2$ and $\alpha<\Gamma_d$, equality holds exactly for the axial cone marks just described with the cap toward the apex, parallel to the base. At $\alpha=\Gamma_d$, equality under the stated cap hypothesis is equivalent to $y$ being the centroid. These cone caps minimize the ordinary cap fraction at the given mark and give equality for every $\alpha\in(0,\Gamma_d]$.

For the minimum ordinary fraction $\alpha_K(y)$ over closed halfspaces containing $y$, the minimum is attained by a cap through $y$, and
$$
\alpha_K(y)\ \ge\ F_d^{-1}(E/V),\qquad
\alpha_K(y)\ \ge\ \Gamma_d\max\left(0,1-\sqrt{\frac{2d}{d+1}(1-E/V)}\right).
$$
The inverse bound is sharp for each $E/V\in(0,1]$ and the second bound is exact for intervals.
title: Sharp projective energy from retained mass and total volume
